title: DeVore's Minneapolis band, audiences and Wild Bill Davison
summary: DeVore says his band has won a Minneapolis following by rhythm and just enough music, rivaling Doc Evans, and praises Wild Bill Davison's attack, tone and phrasing.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: Well, what about... Do you think that your band has had any effect on the Minneapolis listening public?

Oh, absolutely. We've gained a following, you know. And now there's two separate schools. There's Doc Evans School and the Hall Brothers School for listening to music. We've been able to convert a lot of people, not because of musicianship, because we're pretty sure on that, actually. In that respect, I think we kind of resemble the bands down here. We've learned just enough music to do what we want to do. And they haven't gone into any really... gone into the pursuit of the instrument very deeply. But just to play the kind of... you know, the real New Orleans guys, they knew all music. Which is right, I think. But there's the time involved and what you want to do with it. I mean, the requirements for a band these days are so much different than they were back in those days. A person would... I think ideally it would be perfect for a person to learn music top to bottom. But for our purposes, it has been adequate to learn just enough music to do what we wanted to do. For harmony parts and things like that. But the audiences respond to our band for the same reason that they respond to a New Orleans band. The rhythmical angle. Rhythm, rhythm, rhythm. We pound that into everybody in the ensembles to back up a man all the time with riffs. With hot riffs. That's where the swing bands got those from New Orleans bands anyway. And rhythm all the time. And that regards if it's an actual rhythm section man or a horn man. A good New Orleans band to me was a six piece rhythm section. That's why I always looked at it. Not always. I mean, that's... That's the way it evolved into this. As far as my own thing is going. The more I can become familiar with the music. That it would seem like the bands that... In this respect, a band made up of some of the New York guys like Wild Bill. I like Wild Bill. He doesn't play a real classic New Orleans style. But he plays hot and he does this backing up and stuff. And some of the things he made with Cindy Bichet were just wonderful. Cindy Bichet and Jimmy Archie.

Yeah, that's the thing. See, there is again. Wild Bill, to me, is the most creative of the hot school in New York because of his attack and his tone and his phrasing. When he gets down, it always gets down to those three things.
